items.stem: A distributed denial-of-service attack takes a public web service offline for six hours. Investigators confirm no record was read or altered. Which leg of the CIA triad was violated, and is this properly classified as a security incident?

options.text: Availability was violated; yes, an attack-caused outage is a security incident even though nothing was read or changed.
options.why: Availability is a security property in its own right, so denying it through attack is a security incident, not merely an operations problem.

options.text: Nothing was violated — no confidentiality or integrity breach occurred, so the outage is purely an operations matter.
options.why: This is exactly the hesitation the exam exploits: availability is a CIA leg, so an attack-caused outage is a security incident on its own terms.

options.text: Integrity was violated, because the service being unreachable means its data can no longer be trusted.
options.why: Integrity concerns undetected alteration of data; an outage with no record touched does not put integrity in question.

options.text: Confidentiality was violated, since an outage prevents authorised parties from confirming their data is still private.
options.why: Confidentiality concerns unauthorised reading, which an outage with no data accessed does not involve.

items.rationale: The CIA triad classifies a described incident onto confidentiality, integrity or availability. A denial-of-service attack denies availability specifically, and because availability is itself a security property, the resulting outage counts as a security incident rather than only an operational one.

items.stem: An unencrypted nightly backup restores a deleted table correctly after a fault. Which CIA property did the restoration itself demonstrate, and which property does the backup's lack of encryption still leave exposed?

options.text: The restore demonstrated integrity and availability; the unencrypted backup leaves confidentiality exposed.
options.why: Restoring known-good data serves both integrity and availability, but a backup that anyone with access to the media can read still weakens confidentiality.

options.text: The restore demonstrated confidentiality; encryption of the backup file is irrelevant once the restore succeeds.
options.why: A successful restore says nothing about confidentiality, and the guide is explicit that an unencrypted backup weakens exactly that leg.

options.text: The restore demonstrated availability only; a backup is never an integrity control regardless of encryption.
options.why: The guide states a backup restores known-good data and is therefore both an availability and an integrity control.

options.text: The restore demonstrated authentication and authorization, since only a permitted operator could run it.
options.why: Authentication and authorization are not legs of the CIA triad; they belong to the separate AAA trio.

items.rationale: A backup restore serves availability (the service returns) and integrity (the data is known-good), which is exactly why the guide names it an availability-and-integrity control. It is not automatically a confidentiality control, and an unencrypted backup file continues to expose confidentiality even after a clean restore.

items.stem: A user's browser receives a `401 Unauthorized` response, and a colleague reads that as an authorization failure. What is the correct reading, and which of the two processes must succeed before the other can even be evaluated?

options.text: `401` means authentication failed, and authentication must succeed before authorization is evaluated at all.
options.why: HTTP's naming inverts intuition — `401 Unauthorized` is actually an authentication failure — and there is nothing to authorize until an identity is established.

options.text: `401` means authorization failed, since the status name says "Unauthorized" directly.
options.why: This is the naming trap the guide calls out explicitly: `401` is the missing-credentials code, not the permissions code.

options.text: `401` means authorization failed, and authorization is always evaluated first because it determines whether a login prompt is shown.
options.why: Authorization has nothing to evaluate until an identity exists, so it cannot run before authentication regardless of the status code involved.

options.text: `401` reports an accounting failure, since the server could not record who made the request, though accounting has no HTTP status code of its own to report through.
options.why: Accounting is the third A of AAA and records what happened after access is decided; it has no HTTP status code of its own.

items.rationale: Authentication establishes identity and always runs first, because authorization has nothing to evaluate until a subject is known. HTTP's status codes invert the intuitive reading: `401 Unauthorized` is a failed authentication, while `403 Forbidden` is an authenticated request that authorization still refuses.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED, then fixed in place and re-verified against the primary sources listed below; this verdict is the post-fix one. Key is correct and now sourced: RFC 9110 Sec. 15.5.2 states the 401 status code "indicates that the request has not been applied because it lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource", and CSRC term page for authentication gives "verifying the identity of a user, process, or device, often as a prerequisite to allowing access to resources", which is the ordering the key asserts. Defect: no cited source covered HTTP status semantics at all — SP 800-63B-4 has 3 occurrences of "authorization" and no HTTP status codes, and the glossary landing page is empty. Added rfc-9110-http-semantics to the concept sources and replaced the glossary landing page with the authentication/authorization term pages. Distractors o2, o3, o4 are each false and their why text is true.

items.stem: Authentication, accounting and auditing, and multi-factor authentication are often offered as alternatives to one another. Which axis actually separates them?

options.text: When each acts: authentication decides access before it is granted, accounting records what happened afterwards, and MFA strengthens the authentication step rather than adding a further stage.
options.why: NIST defines authentication as verifying identity "often as a prerequisite to allowing access", and audit as the "independent review and examination of records and activities" that follows; MFA acts at the same moment as authentication, only with more than one factor category (SP 800-63B-4).

options.text: How strong each is: accounting is the weakest of the three, authentication is moderate, and MFA is the strongest because it checks more than one factor.
options.why: Accounting is not a weaker authentication — it answers a different question entirely, recording what an already-admitted identity did rather than deciding whether to admit it.

options.text: What each costs to deploy — MFA is the most expensive, authentication moderate, and accounting the cheapest because it only writes log lines.
options.why: Deployment cost does not distinguish them; each answers a different question and acts at a different moment relative to the access decision.

options.text: How widely each is scoped: authentication covers a single system, accounting covers a whole organisation, and MFA covers only privileged accounts.
options.why: Scope of rollout is a deployment choice, not a property of the controls; all three can apply to any account on any number of systems.

items.rationale: The named comparison block separates authentication/authorization, accounting and auditing, and multi-factor authentication by timing: the first pair is preventive and acts before and during access, accounting is detective and acts afterward from records, and MFA is not a fourth A at all — it strengthens the authentication step itself.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED, then fixed in place and re-verified against the primary sources listed below; this verdict is the post-fix one. Rewritten. Re-checked after rewrite: key correct, o2/o3/o4 each false with true why.

items.stem: "Root can do anything on this box" is a statement about which of the two processes, and does root still have to complete the other one first?

options.text: It is an authorization statement, and root still has to authenticate before that authorization ever applies.
options.why: What root may do is a policy question, which is authorization; identity still has to be established first through authentication.

options.text: It is an authentication statement, since being root proves who the user is without any further check.
options.why: This is the second trap the guide names directly: unlimited permission is an authorization property, not proof of identity.

options.text: It is an accounting statement, describing what root has already done on the system.
options.why: Accounting records actions taken after access, whereas this statement describes what root is permitted to do, not a log of what it did.

options.text: It is neither, since root bypasses both authentication and authorization by design on a Linux system.
options.why: Root still authenticates like any other account; what differs is the breadth of what authorization then grants it.

items.rationale: Unlimited permission describes what an identity may do once known, which is authorization. Authentication — proving that the identity really is root — is a separate, prior step that the statement takes for granted rather than replaces.

items.stem: An engineer with legitimate database access quietly exports a customer table over several weeks. No authentication or authorization control was ever bypassed. Which control is positioned to detect this, and why can the first two As of AAA not catch it by design?

options.text: Accounting and auditing, because authentication and authorization only judge whether access is granted, not what a legitimately admitted identity then does with it.
options.why: The insider's access is legitimate, so the preventive controls never engage; only reviewing the record of what was done can surface the exfiltration.

options.text: Multi-factor authentication, because a stronger login would have stopped the export before any rows left the database.
options.why: MFA strengthens proof of identity at login; it does nothing once a legitimately authenticated identity is already acting.

options.text: Authorization, because a permission check is re-evaluated on every row a query returns and would have failed partway through the export.
options.why: Authorization decides access at the point of the request and is not re-run per row, so it never notices a pattern of legitimate reads accumulating over weeks.

options.text: Nothing in AAA addresses this; only network segmentation placed between the analyst and the database can detect a slow export.
options.why: Accounting exists precisely to catch what preventive access controls cannot, so the AAA triad is not blind to this case.

items.rationale: Accounting is the only one of the three As that produces evidence of what an authenticated, authorized identity actually did. It is what makes an insider's legitimate-access misuse reconstructable, since authentication and authorization have already been satisfied and cannot flag it themselves.

items.stem: After an unauthorised change is discovered, a manager proposes "enable auditing" as the fix that prevents it from happening again. What is wrong with that framing?

options.text: Auditing is a detective control; it can establish that the change happened but cannot itself have stopped it, so the preventive fix is an authorization change.
options.why: The guide is explicit that accounting is never a preventive control — offering it as the fix for an unauthorised action mistakes detection for prevention.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; enabling auditing is itself a preventive control, because a system that is watching refuses any action it cannot attribute.
options.why: This is precisely the misconception the guide warns against: accounting only ever establishes that an action occurred, never stops it.

options.text: Auditing is wrong here because the correct fix is always multi-factor authentication, which re-checks the operator's identity before each write.
options.why: MFA strengthens login proof and does not address an authorization problem, which is what an unauthorised change actually is.

options.text: Auditing is wrong because the real gap was in encryption at rest, which would have made the stored record unwritable without the key.
options.why: Encryption at rest protects stored data from being read by someone who obtains the medium; it does not decide who may change a record, which is what an unauthorised change turns on.

items.rationale: Accounting is a detective control: it establishes that an action occurred and by whom, but it cannot itself prevent the action. The preventive remedy for an unauthorised change is tightening authorization, not enabling more logging around it.

items.stem: A server has written detailed access logs for a year, but nobody has ever reviewed them. Has the organisation been auditing its access?

options.text: No. Recording the events is accounting; auditing is the review activity, and records nobody reviews detect nothing.
options.why: The guide separates the two explicitly: accounting is the recording, auditing is the review, and unreviewed logs satisfy only the first.

options.text: Yes — the mere presence of the logs constitutes auditing regardless of whether anyone reads them.
options.why: The guide states this directly as a trap: the presence of logs is not auditing, since unreviewed records detect nothing.

options.text: Yes, because writing the logs already satisfies the authentication requirement for the account that generated them.
options.why: Authentication concerns proving identity at login and has no bearing on whether records are later reviewed.

options.text: No, and the fix is to encrypt the log files rather than to schedule a review.
options.why: Encrypting the logs protects their confidentiality but does not make anyone examine them, which is the actual gap.

items.rationale: Accounting produces the record; auditing is the act of reviewing it. A year of unread logs demonstrates that accounting worked, but auditing — the review that actually detects misuse — never happened.

items.stem: A cron job runs nightly maintenance as root because that was the simplest way to get it working, and nobody has revisited the decision since. What does this violate, and what does that violation actually cost if the job is ever compromised?

options.text: It violates least privilege, and the cost is that a bug in the job becomes a root-level compromise instead of one confined to an unprivileged account.
options.why: Least privilege sets the blast radius of a failure; a root cron job hands an attacker the whole machine instead of one narrow account.

options.text: It is not a violation — least privilege applies only to human accounts, not to cron jobs and other automated processes running under service identities.
options.why: The guide states this directly: a cron job or container running as root is a least-privilege violation even though no person is involved.

options.text: It violates defense in depth, since a single overprivileged job removes one layer from the stack.
options.why: The comparison table draws the line at what defense in depth constrains: the number of independent layers, not how much authority one identity holds.

options.text: It violates accounting, because a root cron job cannot be attributed to a specific person.
options.why: Attribution is an accounting concern, but the described problem is about how much access the job holds, not about who gets credited for its actions.

items.rationale: Least privilege applies to any identity — human or automated — and limits how much a single compromise can reach. A root cron job has no need for that scope, and running it that way turns an ordinary bug into a full machine compromise.

Neither supported the item. Replaced at concept level with the SP 800-53r5 AC-6 reference. Also converted o2 to an em-dash construction so the em-dash tell does not sit only on keys.

items.stem: An administrator elevates through `sudo` for individual commands rather than logging in directly as root for the whole session. Which practice does this illustrate?

options.text: Least privilege, since access above the ordinary account is granted only per command and only for as long as it is needed.
options.why: Per-command elevation is the guide's stated example of least privilege applied to duration as well as scope.

options.text: Defense in depth, because `sudo` adds an independent layer on top of the login itself.
options.why: `sudo` elevation narrows how much authority the account holds at any moment; it does not add a separately-failing barrier on the path in.

options.text: Multi-factor authentication, since a second credential is effectively required for each elevated command.
options.why: Per-command `sudo` elevation does not itself introduce a second, distinct factor category the way MFA does.

options.text: Accounting, because `sudo` records who ran which command.
options.why: Logging elevated commands is a side benefit for accounting, but the practice being described — using ordinary accounts and elevating per command — is what least privilege names.

items.rationale: Least privilege means granting only the access a task requires, for no longer than it needs it. Elevating per command through `sudo` rather than logging in as root applies that idea to duration as well as to scope.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED, then fixed in place and re-verified against the primary sources listed below; this verdict is the post-fix one. items.stem: A service already sits behind a network firewall. A proposal adds a host firewall on the machine itself. What determines whether this counts as a genuine second layer of defense in depth?

options.text: Whether the two fail independently: if a misconfiguration or bypass of the network rule still leaves the host rule enforcing, it is a real second layer.
options.why: SP 800-53r5 warns that replicated protection mechanisms give only illusory additional protection when the mechanisms are similar, because an adversary can attack them in series; independence of failure is what makes a second control a second layer.

options.text: Whether the two run identical rule sets, since matching rules guarantee the second firewall enforces everything the first one does.
options.why: Identical mechanisms are precisely what makes the extra protection illusory — SP 800-53r5 states that if the mechanisms are similar the adversary can simply attack them in series.

options.text: Whether the second firewall sits on a different host — defense in depth counts layers by the number of machines involved.
options.why: Layers are counted by independent failure modes, not by machines; two hosts enforcing the same flawed rule fall together.

options.text: Whether the host firewall improves availability, since layering is only ever a redundancy measure for uptime.
options.why: Layering addresses resistance to compromise rather than uptime, and a firewall can serve confidentiality, integrity or availability depending on what it filters.

items.rationale: Defense in depth is layering independent controls so no single failure exposes the asset. A host firewall enforcing at the machine itself fails for reasons distinct from a network-edge misconfiguration, which is exactly the independence the practice requires — unlike two firewalls duplicating the same rule set at the same boundary.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED, then fixed in place and re-verified against the primary sources listed below; this verdict is the post-fix one. items.stem: A user's login requires a password and a security question. Why does this fail to count as a second layer of defense in depth even though two credentials are checked?

options.text: Both are "something you know," so they fall to the same disclosure and share a failure mode rather than failing independently.
options.why: Two controls that share a failure mode are one layer, not two, and a password plus a security question are both defeated by the same kind of leak.

options.text: It does count, since checking two separate pieces of information is exactly what defense in depth means.
options.why: Counting layers by number of checks rather than by independence of failure is the error the guide's comparison exists to correct.

options.text: It fails because a security question violates least privilege by granting more access than the task requires.
options.why: Least privilege is about how much authority an identity holds once admitted, not about how login credentials are structured.

options.text: It fails because security questions are a form of biometric authentication, which is inherently unreliable as a second factor.
options.why: A security question is a knowledge factor, not a biometric, and the objection here is about shared failure mode rather than factor type.

items.rationale: Defense in depth requires layers to fail for different reasons. A password and a security question are both "something you know" and both fall to the same kind of disclosure, so duplicating the check does not add independence — it duplicates one layer rather than adding a second.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED, then fixed in place and re-verified against the primary sources listed below; this verdict is the post-fix one. items.stem: A request originates from a laptop connected to the corporate VPN. Under a zero-trust architecture, what does that origin grant the request by itself?

options.text: Nothing, since being on the VPN confers no implicit trust; the request is still authenticated and authorized on its own merits.
options.why: Zero trust removes exactly this assumption: network location, including being on a VPN, does not grant access by itself.

options.text: Full access to any resource reachable from that network segment, since the VPN already authenticated the device.
options.why: This is the perimeter-model assumption zero trust exists to remove; VPN membership is not treated as sufficient for access to anything.

options.text: A reduced attack surface — VPN traffic is automatically encrypted end to end.
options.why: Attack surface is about what is reachable at all, a separate concept from whether a request is implicitly trusted by its origin.

options.text: A stronger authentication factor, since VPN connection counts as something you have.
options.why: Being on a network is not treated as an authentication factor in the NIST model; every request is still evaluated against policy independently.

items.rationale: Zero trust grants no request implicit trust based on where it came from. A device being on the VPN or inside the corporate network confers nothing by itself; each request is still authenticated, authorized, and evaluated against policy on its own merits.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED, then fixed in place and re-verified against the primary sources listed below; this verdict is the post-fix one. Key correct and quoted almost verbatim by the source: SP 800-207 states "Zero trust assumes there is no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location (i.e., local area networks versus the internet) or based on asset ownership." Defects: (1) the item cited the empty CSRC glossary landing page and the SP 800-207 abstract landing page rather than the document; /glossary/term/zero-trust-architecture was not reachable. Replaced with the SP 800-207 PDF. (2) o2 carried its own why in its option text; stripped, and an em-dash clause moved onto o3.

items.stem: NIST SP 800-207 describes a policy decision point and a policy enforcement point. What role does each play in a zero-trust architecture?

options.text: The decision point evaluates each request against identity and context; the enforcement point opens, monitors, and terminates the resulting connection.
options.why: That division of labour is exactly how NIST SP 800-207 structures per-request verification: one component decides, the other carries out and continues to police the decision.

options.text: The decision point is a firewall at the network edge, and the enforcement point is the VPN concentrator behind it.
options.why: Zero trust's points are per-request logical roles evaluating identity and context, not a fixed pair of perimeter appliances.

options.text: The decision point grants trust once at login, and the enforcement point re-checks it only if the session is idle for a long period.
options.why: Zero trust re-evaluates trust per request rather than granting it once at login and revisiting it only occasionally.

options.text: The decision point encrypts traffic, and the enforcement point decrypts it at the destination.
options.why: Encryption and decryption describe a cryptographic transport concern, not the policy evaluation and enforcement roles these two points play.

items.stem: A host runs a database listener that no application actually uses. Between removing the listener, patching it, and filtering access to it with a firewall rule, which action reduces attack surface the most, and why?

options.text: Removing the listener, because it eliminates the exposure entirely including flaws nobody has discovered in it yet.
options.why: A service that is not installed cannot be exploited by any vulnerability, discovered or not, which is why removal beats patching or filtering when it is an option.

options.text: Patching it, because an up-to-date service is no longer part of the attack surface.
options.why: Patching fixes one known flaw in software that keeps running, so the exposure remains and the next undiscovered flaw still affects it.

options.text: Filtering it with a firewall rule, because that removes the installed surface just as effectively as uninstalling it.
options.why: A firewall rule reduces reachable surface without reducing installed surface — the service is still present if the rule is ever wrong.

options.text: None of the three matters — nothing can be reduced until a vulnerability scan identifies a specific CVE in the listener.
options.why: Attack surface can be reduced without knowing about any specific flaw; waiting for a named CVE is not required to act.

items.rationale: Attack surface is the total set of points an attacker can interact with, and it is the one quantity reducible without knowing about a specific flaw. Removing an unused service eliminates its exposure entirely, including future vulnerabilities, while patching addresses only a named defect and filtering only reachability.

options.text: Attack surface concerns confidentiality only, while a CVE and its patch always concern availability.
options.why: Neither attack surface nor vulnerability management is tied to one CIA leg; a given flaw can affect any of the three.

options.text: Attack surface is measured by a vulnerability scanner, while a CVE is only ever found by an intrusion detection system.
options.why: A scanner finds known weaknesses including CVEs; an IDS detects live activity, not defects catalogued in advance.

options.text: An enabled account that can still log in even though the person who used it left the team last year.

options.text: A CVE severity score published for a package the host has never installed.
options.why: A score for software that is not present does not touch this host's attack surface at all; nothing here is reachable.

options.text: The retention period configured for the organisation's nightly backups.
options.why: A retention setting governs how long recoverable copies persist and is not a point an attacker can interact with directly.

options.text: The six-step order an incident responder follows once an intrusion is confirmed.
options.why: A response procedure describes what happens after compromise, not a point of possible entry beforehand.

items.stem: A scanner reports a critical vulnerability in a package that is installed but never run, on a host unreachable from any network. Is this necessarily high risk?

options.text: Not necessarily, because risk combines likelihood and impact, and the described conditions drive likelihood toward zero even though the vulnerability is real.
options.why: A severity score describes the flaw in the abstract; the scenario's lack of reachability and execution suppresses the likelihood term that risk actually depends on.

options.text: Yes, because a critical severity score is itself the organisation's risk regardless of deployment context, since the score already accounts for exploitability in the wild.
options.why: A raw scanner list is not a work queue until it is risk-ranked; severity alone ignores whether the flaw is reachable or exploitable in context.

options.text: Yes, because the presence of a vulnerability always implies an active threat targeting it.
options.why: A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is a separate circumstance or actor with the potential to exploit it, and presence of one does not establish the other.

options.text: This cannot be assessed at all without first running a penetration test against the host.
options.why: Risk can be reasoned about from likelihood and impact directly, using the deployment context already given, without requiring an exploitation attempt.

items.rationale: Risk is the combination of likelihood and impact, not the severity score alone. A vulnerability in software that is never run and is unreachable from any network has its likelihood driven far down, so the finding is real but not automatically high risk.

items.stem: Which of the three terms — vulnerability, threat, risk — is the only one that carries a magnitude, and what does removing any one of the three do to it?

options.text: Only risk carries a magnitude, and removing any one of the three collapses it, so patching the vulnerability, blocking the threat's access, or reducing the impact all work.
options.why: SP 800-30r1 determines risk as "typically a function of the degree of harm and likelihood of harm occurring" given the potential for threats exploiting vulnerabilities, so removing any factor in that relationship collapses the resulting risk.

options.text: Threat carries the magnitude, since an actor's capability and intent set the scale of what can happen regardless of the flaw.
options.why: It is risk, not threat, that is expressed as a magnitude of likelihood and impact combined; a threat is a circumstance or actor, not a scored quantity.

options.text: Vulnerability carries the magnitude, expressed through its CVSS score.
options.why: CVSS scores a specific catalogued defect's severity, which is a different measurement from the likelihood-and-impact combination that defines risk.

options.text: All three carry the same magnitude, since they are used interchangeably in practice and describe one underlying exposure viewed from three different angles.
options.why: NIST keeps the three distinct: a vulnerability is a weakness, a threat is a circumstance or actor with the potential to exploit it, and only risk is expressed as a magnitude combining likelihood and harm.

items.rationale: A vulnerability is a weakness and a threat is a potential exploiter — neither carries a magnitude on its own. Risk is the combination of likelihood and impact, and removing any one of the three factors — patching the weakness, blocking the threat's access path, or reducing impact through segmentation and backups — collapses the resulting risk.

items.stem: A login requires a password, then a one-time code delivered by SMS. An attacker runs a real-time phishing relay that captures both and logs in immediately. Did MFA fail here, and what would have stopped this specific attack?

options.text: MFA reduced but did not end the risk; only a phishing-resistant authenticator such as a FIDO2 security key breaks a real-time relay.
options.why: An SMS code is a genuine second factor but is not phishing-resistant, so a relay that captures and replays it in real time defeats it — a security key's response is bound to the real site and cannot be relayed the same way.

options.text: MFA fully succeeded, since two distinct factor categories were checked and that is sufficient against any credential attack by definition.
options.why: The guide states plainly that MFA reduces phishing damage but does not end it, because a relay can capture and replay a code the user was tricked into providing.

options.text: MFA did not apply here at all, since a password and an SMS code are both "something you know."
options.why: A password is something you know and an SMS code relies on possession of the phone, so this is genuinely two distinct factor categories, unlike a password plus a security question.

options.text: The fix is authorization review, since the account should never have been permitted to log in from a new location.
options.why: The failure here is at authentication — the attacker proved possession of valid credentials — not a subsequent authorization policy decision.

items.rationale: SMS one-time codes are a real second factor but not a phishing-resistant one: a real-time relay captures and replays them before the code expires. Phishing-resistant authenticators such as FIDO2 security keys bind their response to the legitimate site, which is what actually stops this attack.

verification.reasoning: Key correct and directly sourced: SP 800-63B-4 states "Out-of-band authentication is not phishing-resistant", and its AAL table lists phishing resistance as required only at AAL3, where the authenticator "SHALL have a non-exportable private key and SHALL provide phishing resistance" — which is what a FIDO2 security key supplies and an SMS code does not. o2 is false (two categories do not confer phishing resistance); o3 is false and its why correctly separates a possession-based SMS code from a knowledge factor; o4 is false and its why is true. Both cited sources checked; SP 800-63B-4 carries the claim, and no option depends on the LF page.

items.stem: NIST SP 800-63B requires two distinct factor categories at AAL2. Which of these logins actually satisfies that requirement?

options.text: A password plus a fingerprint compared against the stored reference on the user's registered device.
options.why: The password is something you know and the biometric bound to a device is something you have plus something you are, giving two genuinely distinct categories.

options.text: A password plus a memorised security question, since two separate credentials are checked.
options.why: Both a password and a security question are "something you know," so this is one factor category checked twice, not two categories.

options.text: A fingerprint scan alone, with no accompanying device or credential.
options.why: The guide states a biometric on its own is not treated as an authenticator; it always accompanies the device holding it, so this is not two factors or even one complete one.

options.text: Two different passwords entered in sequence for extra assurance.
options.why: Two passwords are both "something you know," so this is a single factor category checked twice rather than genuine multi-factor authentication.

items.rationale: MFA requires evidence from two or more distinct factor categories: something you know, something you have, and something you are. A password paired with a device-bound biometric spans two categories; a password paired with a second knowledge item, however different it feels, is one category checked twice.

Key correct and sourced: SP 800-63B-4 requires "Biometrics SHALL only be used as part of multi-factor authentication with a physical authenticator (i.e., 'something you have')", so a password plus a device-bound biometric comparison spans two distinct categories, while o3 (biometric alone) is excluded by the same sentence and o2/o4 are one category checked twice. items.stem: Two users choose the same password on a system that stores salted SHA-256 hashes. An attacker steals the database. Why does salting alone not make this table safe against a determined attacker?

options.text: The salt defeats precomputation and stops the two users producing identical hashes, but SHA-256 is fast, so each individual guess is still cheap to try.
options.why: Salting solves uniqueness and rainbow-table reuse, not speed; a deliberately slow function such as Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 is what raises the per-guess cost.

options.text: It is not safe because the salt must be kept secret and this system almost certainly stored it in the clear next to the hash.
options.why: The salt does not need to be secret — its job is uniqueness, and storing it in the clear alongside the hash is correct and expected, not the flaw here.

options.text: It is not safe because SHA-256 is reversible with the right key, unlike a true one-way hash.
options.why: SHA-256 has no key and is not reversible; the weakness described is its speed against brute-force guessing, not reversibility.

options.text: It is not safe because this describes encryption, not hashing, and encryption always requires a shared key an attacker can also steal.
options.why: Storing a one-way digest with a salt is hashing, not encryption; there is no key involved and nothing here is reversible.

items.rationale: A salt exists to prevent precomputed rainbow tables and to stop identical passwords producing identical hashes across accounts; it does not slow down the hash function itself. SHA-256 is deliberately fast, so a salted SHA-256 password table still falls quickly to an attacker who can attempt guesses at speed — the fix is a deliberately slow, memory-hard function, not more salting.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED, then fixed in place and re-verified against the primary sources listed below; this verdict is the post-fix one. Key correct and sourced twice: SP 800-63B-4 requires passwords to be "salted and hashed using a suitable password hashing scheme" taking "a password, a salt, and a cost factor as inputs", whose purpose is "to make each password guess more expensive", and the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet names Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt and PBKDF2 for exactly that work factor — salting addresses uniqueness and precomputation, not per-guess cost. o2's why is true (OWASP states the salt need not be secret and is stored alongside the hash). Defect: o3 carried its own why in its option text; stripped.

items.stem: A support engineer claims the application can display a user's existing password on request, and calls this "hashing it for display." What does this claim actually reveal about how the password is stored?

options.text: The password is stored reversibly, not hashed at all, since hashing has no decryption step and cannot be shown back to anyone.
options.why: The guide states this exactly as the trap: a system that can show a user their existing password is storing it reversibly, which is not hashing regardless of what it is called internally.

options.text: The password is correctly hashed with a fast algorithm, since fast hashing allows quick redisplay when requested.
options.why: Hash function speed has nothing to do with whether the original input can be recovered — a one-way hash cannot be reversed regardless of how fast it runs.

options.text: The password is stored with a pepper instead of a salt, which permits recovery when combined with the secret pepper value.
options.why: A pepper is an additional secret layered on top of hashing, not a mechanism that makes a one-way function reversible.

options.text: The password is stored using asymmetric encryption, which allows the application to decrypt it with the matching private key.
options.why: Nothing in the claim describes a key pair, and password storage is expected to be one-way hashing, not any form of encryption at all.

items.rationale: Hashing is one-way by construction: there is no key and no decryption step, so nothing that can be displayed back to a user was ever properly hashed. A system that can show an existing password is storing it reversibly, and calling that step "hashing" does not change what actually happened to the data.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED, then fixed in place and re-verified against the primary sources listed below; this verdict is the post-fix one. Key correct: SP 800-63B-4 requires passwords stored "in a form that is resistant to offline attacks", salted and hashed, and the OWASP cheat sheet separates hashing from encryption precisely on the point that hashing is one-way and cannot be reversed — so a system that can redisplay a password is not hashing it. o3's why is true (OWASP describes a pepper as an extra secret applied on top of hashing, not a recovery mechanism). Defect: o2 carried its own why in its option text; stripped.

items.stem: An employee leaves the organisation. Under SSO, what single action removes their access to every participating application?

options.text: Disabling the account at the identity provider, since applications trust its assertion rather than running their own login.
options.why: Centralising the authentication decision at the identity provider is exactly what makes offboarding a single, reliable action under SSO.

options.text: Nothing single-handed works; each participating application must have its own account disabled separately.
options.why: This describes password synchronisation, sometimes called same-sign-on, where each application still runs its own login — SSO's point is precisely to avoid that per-application cleanup.

options.text: Revoking the employee's MFA enrolment, since SSO and MFA are the same control.
options.why: SSO changes how many times a user authenticates, not how strongly; MFA is a separate, complementary control enforced at the identity provider.

options.text: Rotating the shared password used across every application.
options.why: Under SSO there is no password at the application to rotate — only an assertion from the identity provider to validate.

items.rationale: Under SSO, applications trust the identity provider's signed assertion about who the user is rather than running their own login. Disabling the account at that one central point removes access everywhere at once, which is what makes offboarding reliable.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED, then fixed in place and re-verified against the primary sources listed below; this verdict is the post-fix one. Key is correct but the item had no supporting source whatsoever: its only two citations were lf-objectives-2025 (the LFCA program-changes page, zero occurrences of "single sign") and the CSRC glossary landing page, which serves no definitions and 404s at /glossary/term/single-sign-on. This process is sometimes known as single sign-on", and describes the RP consuming an IdP assertion rather than running its own login — which is what makes disabling the account at the IdP a single effective offboarding action. items.stem: A security architect wants to reduce how many separate passwords staff must choose and remember. Does deploying SSO by itself also make each individual login stronger?

options.text: No. SSO reduces credential sprawl and centralises the control point, but it changes how many times a user authenticates, not how strongly.
options.why: The guide is explicit that SSO and MFA are offered as alternatives on the exam precisely because SSO alone does not add authentication strength.

options.text: Yes, since consolidating logins into one identity provider automatically enforces a stronger authenticator everywhere.
options.why: SSO centralises where authentication happens; strengthening it to require MFA is a separate, deliberate decision enforced at the identity provider.

options.text: Yes, because SSO always requires public-key authentication instead of a password.
options.why: SSO does not mandate any particular authenticator type; what it changes is how many separate logins the user performs.

options.text: No, and SSO actually weakens security in every deployment by design.
options.why: SSO concentrates risk in one login, which is exactly why MFA is enforced alongside it rather than a reason to call SSO weaker in every case.

items.rationale: SSO reduces the number of separate passwords a user manages and centralises the control point for offboarding, but it does not by itself make any single authentication event stronger. Putting every application behind one login concentrates risk there, which is why MFA is enforced at the identity provider alongside SSO rather than replaced by it.

items.stem: An engineer runs `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "laptop"` and then needs to install the resulting public key on a remote server they can currently only reach with a password. Which command installs it correctly?

options.text: `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@host`, appending the public half to the remote account's `authorized_keys`
options.why: `ssh-copy-id` appends the named public key to the remote account's `authorized_keys`, and it needs a working login such as the still-enabled password the first time.

options.text: `ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, loading the key so the remote server can pick it up on the next connection
options.why: `ssh-add` loads a private key into the agent on the local machine and installs nothing on the remote host, so the server still holds no copy of the public key.

options.text: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "laptop"` run a second time directly on the remote server
options.why: `ssh-keygen` generates a new key pair; it does not install an existing public key anywhere, and running it again would just create an unrelated pair on the server.

options.text: `gpg --verify ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@host`, verifying the key's signature against the remote account
options.why: `gpg --verify` checks a signature over a file against a signing key; it has no role in installing an SSH public key into a remote account.

items.rationale: `ssh-keygen` generates the key pair; `ssh-copy-id` installs the *public* half into the remote account's `authorized_keys`, and needs a working login — typically the still-enabled password — the first time it runs. Copying the private key instead of the `.pub` file is the classic and dangerous mix-up.

items.stem: During SSH's publickey authentication, what does the client actually transmit to the server, and why does this resist replay in a way a password does not?

options.text: A signature over session-specific data, never the private key or anything reusable, so an attacker recording the exchange gains nothing replayable.
options.why: RFC 4252 has the client sign a session-specific challenge with the private key and send only the signature, unlike a password which the server must receive directly.

options.text: The private key itself, encrypted with the server's public key so only that server can read it.
options.why: The private key never leaves the client under any circumstance; what crosses the wire is a signature, not the key in any form.

options.text: A one-time password derived from the key pair, refreshed every thirty seconds like a hardware token.
options.why: SSH publickey authentication is not a time-based one-time code scheme; it signs session-specific data at the moment of connection.

options.text: A hash of the password the user would otherwise have typed, computed locally before sending.
options.why: There is no password involved in publickey authentication at all; the mechanism authenticates by proving possession of the private key, not by hashing a secret.

items.rationale: SSH's publickey method has the client sign a session-specific challenge with its private key and send only the resulting signature. Because the signature is bound to that session, an attacker who records the exchange gains nothing replayable — unlike a password, which the server must receive and could log, leak, or have phished.

items.stem: A TLS 1.3 handshake performs an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange and a certificate-based signature over that handshake, and then switches to a different kind of cryptography for the actual application data. Why does the protocol switch rather than using one kind throughout?

options.text: Asymmetric cryptography authenticates the peer and agrees a fresh key without a pre-shared secret; symmetric cryptography is fast enough to carry the bulk traffic that follows.
options.why: The two families solve different problems, and TLS uses each for the one it solves: asymmetric for identity and key agreement, symmetric for speed on the actual data.

options.text: It switches because asymmetric encryption is strictly stronger and the handshake only needs the weaker symmetric form for routine traffic.
options.why: Asymmetric is not "stronger" than symmetric; the guide notes key sizes are not even comparable across the two families, and each solves a different problem.

options.text: It switches because symmetric cryptography is what proves the server's identity, while asymmetric only ever protects confidentiality.
options.why: This reverses the roles — the certificate and asymmetric handshake are what authenticate the server, not the symmetric traffic keys.

options.text: It switches because hashing replaces asymmetric cryptography once the handshake completes, since hashing is faster still and a digest of the traffic keys is all the record layer needs to keep the channel confidential afterwards.
options.why: Hashing is a separate, one-way primitive used for integrity, not a substitute for the symmetric encryption that protects the application data itself.

items.rationale: Symmetric and asymmetric cryptography exist together rather than one replacing the other because they solve different problems: asymmetric cryptography authenticates the peer and agrees a fresh key without a pre-shared secret, and the resulting symmetric key then protects the actual traffic efficiently. TLS's handshake-then-bulk-data structure is this division made concrete.

RFC 8446 Section 2 separates the two jobs explicitly: (EC)DHE is one of three key-exchange modes, while authentication is carried by Certificate and CertificateVerify, "a signature over the entire handshake using the private key corresponding to the public key in the Certificate message". The key and all three distractors were correct as authored and are unchanged; only the stem was wrong. items.stem: Symmetric-versus-asymmetric encryption, hashing, and password hashing and salting are compared as a trio. Which single property most cleanly separates encryption from both kinds of hashing in that comparison?

options.text: Reversibility, since encryption is meant to be undone by whoever holds the right key, while both hashing forms are one-way by construction.
options.why: The comparison table names reversibility and speed as the separating axis, and reversibility is what cleanly distinguishes encryption from either hashing form.

options.text: Key involvement — encryption never uses a key, while both hashing forms require one.
options.why: This reverses the table: encryption involves a shared key or a key pair, while general hashing uses no key at all and password hashing uses a salt and work factor instead of a key.

options.text: Output length — encryption always produces a longer output than either hashing form.
options.why: The comparison does not turn on output length at all; it turns on whether the transformation can be undone.

options.text: Algorithm age — encryption algorithms are all newer than the hash functions used for either purpose, a property the comparison table does not track at all when separating the three primitives from one another.
options.why: Relative age of the algorithms is not a property the guide's table tracks or that determines which primitive to choose for a job.

items.rationale: The comparison's separating axis is reversibility and speed: encryption is designed to be undone by the key holder, while general hashing is one-way and fast and password hashing is one-way and deliberately slow. Using a general-purpose hash where a password hash belongs, or expecting either hash to be reversible, is the error the table exists to prevent.

verification.reasoning: Key o1 (reversibility) holds against SP 800-57 Pt1 Rev5, which defines encryption as recoverable with the right key and states the one-way property of an approved hash function; the NIST glossary hash function entry states it directly ("(One-way) It is computationally infeasible to find any input that maps to any new pre-specified output"). o2 is false and inverted: encryption uses a key, general hashing uses none. o3 is false: a stream cipher ciphertext is the length of its plaintext, which can be shorter than a fixed 256-bit digest, so encryption does not "always" produce longer output. o4 is false: algorithm age is not a selection axis. No distractor is defensible as a second answer. Citation note: the cited nist-sp-800-57p1r5 landing page carries only an abstract; the substance is in the linked NIST.SP.800-57pt1r5.pdf, which was fetched and read.

items.stem: A service enables HTTPS on its public endpoint. Does that protect a stolen backup tape holding the same data?

options.text: No, because HTTPS protects data crossing the network, and a stolen backup tape is a data-at-rest exposure that a separate control must cover.
options.why: Encryption in transit and encryption at rest are separate controls covering separate exposures, and one does not substitute for the other.

options.text: Yes, because encrypting the connection also encrypts every copy of the data that connection ever carried, including anything later written to disk from it.
options.why: The guide states directly that HTTPS on the front end does nothing for a stolen backup tape; the two controls do not overlap that way.

options.text: Yes, because TLS certificates also authenticate whoever physically holds the backup media.
options.why: A TLS certificate authenticates a network peer during a connection; it has no bearing on who later holds a piece of offline storage media.

options.text: No, but only because the backup was compressed rather than encrypted, which is a separate deficiency.
options.why: Compression status is unrelated to the actual gap here, which is that encryption in transit and encryption at rest are two distinct controls, neither implying the other.

items.rationale: Encryption at rest protects stored data — disks, backups, object storage; encryption in transit protects data moving across a network. HTTPS on a public endpoint says nothing about whether a backup tape is encrypted, since the two controls address separate exposures and neither substitutes for the other.

verification.reasoning: Key o1 holds. SP 800-57 Pt1 Rev5 Sec 6.2 names the three states verbatim — information is either "in transit", "at rest", or "in use" — and prescribes protection separately for each, so in-transit protection does not cover stored media. RFC 8446 Sec 1 scopes TLS to the channel between two communicating peers. o2 is false on that basis; o3 is false, a TLS certificate binds a key to a network peer name (RFC 5280 Sec 3.2) and says nothing about custody of media; o4 names compression, which is irrelevant. items.stem: A finance application runs on a fully patched host with LUKS-encrypted disks and HTTPS on every connection. An attacker exploits an application bug and reads live records from memory. Which exposure was neither control designed to address?

options.text: Data in use, since a compromised running process reads the unlocked filesystem and live memory normally, and neither at-rest nor in-transit encryption applies there.
options.why: At rest and in transit are the two named controls, and both leave data being actively processed by a compromised application outside their coverage.

options.text: Data at rest, since the LUKS volume should have prevented any process from reading its contents.
options.why: Full disk encryption protects data when the volume is locked or the hardware is lost; once the volume is unlocked and the system is running, files are readable to permitted processes as normal.

options.text: Data in transit, since the application bug must have exposed the TLS session key over the network, though nothing in the scenario describes interception of network traffic, only a compromise reading memory directly on the host itself.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario describes a network interception; the compromise reads memory directly on the host, which is outside what in-transit encryption covers in either case.

options.text: None — HTTPS plus LUKS together cover every stage data passes through.
options.why: The pair covers storage and network transit specifically, and the guide names a third stage, data in use, that neither one reaches.

items.rationale: Encryption at rest and encryption in transit are two separate controls, and both stop short of data being actively processed. A compromised running application reads the unlocked filesystem and live memory as any permitted process would, which is why data in use is the exposure neither control was built to close.

verification.reasoning: Key o1 (data in use) holds: SP 800-57 Pt1 Rev5 Sec 6.2 names "in use" as the third state alongside in transit and at rest, and notes a key in use resides inside a cryptographic module while the process holds it — the compromised-process case sits outside both other controls. o2 is false and its why is accurate (an unlocked LUKS volume reads normally; the cryptsetup FAQ Sec 6 records that a volume key can be extracted from a still-open container). o3 is false, nothing in the scenario intercepts network traffic. o4 is false because the third state exists. No second defensible answer. Dead-citation pass 2026-08-19 (resource-security-proc): nist-csrc-glossary dropped at concept level (the /glossary root is a search shell with zero definitions). This item's key was already carried by SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 Sec. 6.2 and the cryptsetup FAQ, both of which were read at verification time; nothing in the item depended on the glossary root. Verdict unchanged.

items.stem: A publisher lists SHA-256 digests for a downloaded ISO. Which command checks the local file against that list, and what does a match actually prove?

options.text: `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`, which proves only that the bytes received match the bytes that were hashed, nothing about who produced them
options.why: `sha256sum -c` reads a file of previously recorded digests and reports OK or FAILED, and a digest match by itself establishes integrity, not origin.

options.text: `md5sum -c SHA256SUMS`, which is interchangeable with `sha256sum` since both compute a digest
options.why: `md5sum` computes MD5 digests, not SHA-256, and MD5 is broken for collision resistance; it would not correctly validate a SHA256SUMS file at all.

options.text: `gpg --verify SHA256SUMS`, which confirms the file's contents are correct without needing a signature
options.why: `gpg --verify` checks a cryptographic signature against a key, a different operation from comparing digests, and it requires an actual signature file to check against.

options.text: `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`, which proves the publisher themselves produced the file and not an impersonator, because a digest list of this kind can only be generated by whoever holds the publisher’s release key.
options.why: A checksum proves only that the bytes match a value; it says nothing about who produced that value, which is what a signature is for.

items.rationale: `sha256sum -c` compares a locally computed digest against a file of previously recorded ones and reports OK or FAILED per entry. A match tells you the bytes you received are the bytes that were hashed — integrity — but says nothing about who produced them, since a digest carries no signature and no key.

items.stem: A support ticket asks for a file to be "decrypted" from its SHA-256 hash so the original contents can be recovered. What is wrong with the request?

options.text: There is no such operation; hashing has no key and is one-way by construction, so the original input cannot be recovered from the digest.
options.why: The guide states directly that "decrypt the hash" is never the answer, because a digest carries no key and the function cannot be inverted.

options.text: The request is valid, but only `md5sum` supports reversal, not `sha256sum`.
options.why: Neither MD5 nor SHA-256 is reversible; both are one-way hash functions regardless of which is used.

options.text: The request is valid if the correct salt is supplied along with the digest.
options.why: A salt applies to password hashing to prevent identical inputs producing identical outputs; it does not make any hash function reversible.

options.text: The request is valid, since `gpg --verify` can recover the original file from a signed digest, because the signature packet embeds a compressed copy of whatever was signed alongside the digest itself.
options.why: `gpg --verify` checks a signature against a file; it has no capability to reconstruct a file's contents from a hash of it.

items.rationale: A hash is a one-way function: the same input always produces the same fixed-length digest, but there is no operation, key, or salt that recovers the input from the digest. "Decrypt the hash" describes something hashing was never designed to do.

items.stem: A browser accepts a self-signed certificate presented by an internal tool, and traffic to it is fully encrypted. A developer argues the warning was pointless since encryption is working. What does the certificate authority actually add that a self-signed certificate lacks?

options.text: Third-party attestation that the public key really belongs to the named host; a self-signed certificate encrypts exactly as well, but nothing vouches for the binding.
options.why: The guide is explicit that a self-signed certificate encrypts identically to a CA-issued one; what it lacks is a third party attesting to the identity binding.

options.text: Stronger encryption, since a CA-issued certificate always uses a longer key than a self-signed one, because the issuing CA replaces the requested public key with one drawn from its own approved key sizes.
options.why: Key strength is independent of who signs the certificate; a self-signed certificate can use exactly the same key length as a CA-issued one.

options.text: Proof that the site's operator is honest and the content served is trustworthy.
options.why: A CA attests that a public key belongs to a named host, not that the host's operator or content deserves the visitor's trust.

options.text: A guarantee that the connection will never expire or need renewal.
options.why: Every certificate, self-signed or CA-issued, carries a validity window and eventually needs renewal; a CA does not remove that requirement.

items.rationale: A certificate binds a public key to an identity, and a CA vouches for that binding by signing it. A self-signed certificate encrypts a connection exactly as well as a CA-issued one — what it lacks is a third party the client already trusts attesting that the key really belongs to the claimed name, which is why browsers warn about it.

verification.reasoning: Key o1 holds against RFC 5280 Sec 3.2: a certificate binds a public key to a subject and "the binding is asserted by having a trusted CA digitally sign each certificate" — the attestation, not the encryption, is what the CA supplies. o2 is false: key size is a certificate field independent of the signer. o3 is false: RFC 5280 asserts a name-to-key binding, not any judgement about the operator or content. o4 is false: RFC 5280 Sec 4.1.2.5 makes a validity window mandatory in every certificate, self-signed included. No second defensible answer. Shape fix on re-check: distractor o2 carried a paraphrase of its own why appended to its text; replaced with a false clause of comparable length, key untouched.

items.stem: A certificate chain runs from a leaf certificate through an intermediate CA to a root certificate that signed itself. Why does the client still trust that root?

options.text: Because the root is already present in the client's trust store as a trust anchor, not because of its own self-signature.
options.why: The root's trustworthiness comes from being included in the operating system's or browser's trust store, since a self-signature alone proves nothing about the signer's honesty.

options.text: Because a root certificate's self-signature is cryptographically stronger than any other signature in the chain, when a self-signature proves nothing about the signer's honesty regardless of how the signature itself is constructed.
options.why: Self-signing is not a stronger form of signature; the root's authority comes entirely from being pre-installed as a trust anchor, not from the signature's mathematics.

options.text: Because TLS 1.3 automatically re-verifies every root certificate against a central registry during the handshake.
options.why: TLS validates the chain against certificates already in the local trust store; it does not consult a central registry during the handshake.

options.text: Because the intermediate CA's signature alone is sufficient, and the root is not actually checked.
options.why: Validation walks the whole chain up to a trust anchor; a chain that never reaches one already in the store fails, however well-formed the intermediate signature is.

items.rationale: A root certificate's trust does not come from its own signature — it signed itself, which proves nothing on its own. It comes from being a trust anchor already present in the operating system's or browser's trust store; a chain that terminates anywhere else fails no matter how well-formed it is.

verification.reasoning: Key o1 holds against RFC 5280 Sec 6.1: "The trust anchor is an input to the algorithm", and Sec 6.1.1 notes that when a trust anchor is supplied as a self-signed certificate, that certificate "is not included as part of the prospective certification path" — the root is trusted because it is the anchor, not because it signed itself. o2 is false: a self-signature is an ordinary signature. o3 is false: path validation runs against locally held anchor information, with no central registry consulted during the handshake (RFC 8446 Sec 4.4.2 defers certificate validation to the endpoint). o4 is false: Sec 6.1 requires the path to terminate at a trust anchor. No second defensible answer.

items.stem: An engineer trained on LFS200 refers to a service's "SSL certificate" and proposes enabling "SSL" for a new internal API. What is wrong with the terminology, and does it matter for the traffic described?

options.text: SSL is TLS's obsolete predecessor and must not be enabled; the object commonly called an "SSL certificate" is an X.509 certificate used by TLS, which is what should be configured instead.
options.why: RFC 7568 states "SSLv3 MUST NOT be used" and requires that negotiation of SSLv3 from any version of TLS be prohibited; the object usually called an "SSL certificate" is the X.509 certificate profiled by RFC 5280 and consumed by TLS.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; SSL and TLS are simply two names in current use for the identical current protocol.
options.why: SSL is an obsolete predecessor to TLS, not an alternate name for the same current protocol, and offering it as a current choice is the trap the guide names directly.

options.text: The terminology only matters for web traffic; an internal API that is not HTTP can safely use SSL, because SSL and TLS diverge only at the HTTP layer and share an identical record format below it.
options.why: TLS is not web-only and is used across SMTP, IMAP, LDAP and database protocols, but that does not make the obsolete SSL protocol an acceptable substitute for any of them.

options.text: The terminology is fine because TLS is a transport protocol that replaced TCP for encrypted connections.
options.why: TLS runs on top of an already-established reliable transport such as TCP rather than replacing it, which is a separate error from the SSL naming issue.

items.rationale: "SSL" names TLS's obsolete predecessor, deprecated by RFC 7568, while the object people call an "SSL certificate" is simply an X.509 certificate used by TLS. LFS200 discusses SSL and never uses the term TLS at all, which is why an engineer trained on that course carries a real vocabulary gap into an exam that expects the current name.

The option text is correct and unchanged — RFC 7568 Sec 3 states "SSLv3 MUST NOT be used" and Sec 1 records that SSLv3 is TLS's predecessor — but the authored rationale asserted that the exam expects TLS by name and that LFS200's own material never uses the term. Neither claim is checkable against any fetchable primary source, and the second is a claim about licensed course material. Replaced with the RFC 7568 requirement and the RFC 5280 certificate profile. items.stem: A site serves malware over a connection with a perfectly valid, correctly configured TLS certificate. What does the padlock in the browser actually indicate in this case?

options.text: An authenticated, encrypted channel to the named host, and nothing about whether the content served over it is safe or the operator is trustworthy.
options.why: HTTPS protects the channel, not the endpoint; a compromised or malicious server can serve harmful content over a perfectly valid TLS connection.

options.text: That the site has passed a security review and its content has been scanned for malware.
options.why: A certificate attests to a key-to-name binding through the CA, not to any review or scan of the site's content.

options.text: That the connection is immune to man-in-the-middle interception for the rest of the session, when the padlock only reflects the current handshake and says nothing about interception risk for the remainder of the session.
options.why: The padlock reflects that the current handshake authenticated the peer; it says nothing about future compromise of the endpoint delivering malware over that same valid channel.

options.text: That the server is running the current TLS 1.3 protocol version rather than an older one.
options.why: The padlock does not itself distinguish protocol version; a connection can be encrypted under an older TLS version and still show the same indicator.

items.rationale: TLS protects the channel between client and server — encrypting it, protecting it from tampering, and authenticating the server via its certificate. It says nothing about the honesty of what that server chooses to send, so a valid padlock and malicious content are entirely compatible.

verification.reasoning: Key o1 holds: RFC 8446 Sec 1 scopes TLS to a channel that is authenticated to the peer and confidential in transit, and RFC 5280 Sec 3.2 scopes the certificate to a key-to-name binding asserted by a CA. Neither speaks to the safety of what is served. o2 is false: no scan or review is attested. o3 is false: RFC 8446 Sec 2 authenticates the handshake, and endpoint compromise afterwards is outside it. o4 is false: the padlock does not encode a version, and RFC 8446 Appendix D preserves interoperability with earlier TLS versions on the same URI scheme. No second defensible answer.

items.stem: A browser reports a certificate problem on a service that changed in no other way overnight. The certificate's `notAfter` date is still weeks away, but the hostname in the certificate does not match the address requested. What is the correct fix, and is renewal the right one?

options.text: Reissue the certificate with the correct name; renewal alone would not fix a hostname mismatch, since the dates were never the problem.
options.why: A hostname mismatch, an untrusted chain, and clock skew all produce a similar-looking warning to expiry but need different remediations, and reissuing with the right name is what a mismatch actually requires.

options.text: Renew the certificate, since every certificate warning is ultimately an expiry problem regardless of what the browser reports.
options.why: Renewing fixes expiry and nothing else; the guide is explicit that several distinct validation failures produce a similar warning and each needs its own fix.

options.text: Install the missing intermediate certificate, since that is always the cause when the leaf certificate itself looks otherwise correct, and a gap in the chain is what makes a browser report the presented name as unrecognised.
options.why: A missing intermediate is one distinct cause among several, but the symptom described — the requested name not appearing in the certificate — points specifically at a hostname mismatch, not a broken chain.

options.text: Correct the client's clock, since a skewed clock is the most common cause of a certificate warning.
options.why: Clock skew produces a warning about the validity window, not about the hostname the certificate presents, so it does not match the symptom described here.

items.rationale: Expiry, a hostname mismatch, an untrusted or incomplete chain, and clock skew all produce browser warnings that look alike to a user but need different fixes: renew, reissue with the correct name, install the CA or missing intermediate, or correct the clock respectively. A mismatch specifically needs reissue, since the dates were never the fault here.

The item turns entirely on a hostname mismatch being a distinct validation failure from expiry, and RFC 5280 does not specify hostname verification at all — its only uses of "host name" are in the name-constraints and URI sections. The document that specifies matching the requested name against the certificate is RFC 9525 (which obsoletes RFC 6125): Sec 6.1, "The client MUST construct a list of acceptable reference identifiers", and Sec 6.3, matching the DNS domain name portion against a DNS-ID. Re-cited to RFC 9525, with RFC 5280 retained for the validity window (Sec 4.1.2.5) and path construction (Sec 6.1) that the distractors turn on. items.stem: A certificate expires at midnight and the connection begins failing outright at that moment. Has the data crossing that connection become unencrypted?

options.text: No. An expired certificate still encrypts perfectly well; what has failed is trust, and the client refuses the connection rather than downgrading it.
options.why: Expiry invalidates trust in the certificate, not the cryptography itself, so "the connection is unencrypted" is the wrong reading of the failure.

options.text: Yes, since an expired certificate can no longer perform any cryptographic operation.
options.why: The guide states directly that this is the wrong reading of the warning; encryption is unaffected by expiry, only trust in the certificate is.

options.text: Yes, because expiry automatically reverts the connection to the deprecated SSL protocol as a fallback, and SSL performs no validity check of its own, so the session continues under the keys already agreed.
options.why: There is no automatic protocol downgrade on expiry; a client that rejects an expired certificate simply refuses to connect at all.

options.text: This cannot be determined without first checking whether the certificate authority itself has been compromised.
options.why: CA compromise is a separate, unrelated failure; an ordinary expiry needs no such investigation to explain the outage.

items.rationale: Expiry is entirely predictable and is the most common cause of a sudden, total outage, but it is a failure of trust, not of cryptography. An expired certificate still encrypts perfectly well; the client simply refuses to proceed because it can no longer vouch for the identity behind the connection.

verification.reasoning: Key o1 holds. RFC 5280 Sec 4.1.2.5 defines the validity period as "the time interval during which the CA warrants that it will maintain information about the status of the certificate" — an expiry is a statement about warranted trust, not about the cryptography, and RFC 8446 Sec 4.4.2.4 leaves the client to abort rather than continue unauthenticated. o2 is false on that basis. o3 is false: no protocol downgrade to SSLv3 exists to fall back to, and RFC 7568 prohibits negotiating it in any case. o4 is false: CA compromise is a separate condition, handled by revocation (RFC 5280 Sec 5), not by ordinary expiry. No second defensible answer. Shape fix: distractor o3 carried its own rationale spliced onto the end of its text, announcing its own wrongness; replaced with a false clause of comparable length so the option stays wrong on substance rather than on shape, without shortening the key.

items.stem: A laptop with a LUKS-encrypted disk is stolen while powered off. What does full disk encryption actually protect here, and is the running-and-unlocked case the same?

options.text: It protects the data because the volume is locked without the key; while the machine was running and unlocked, the same files were readable to any permitted process.
options.why: Full disk encryption is the control that survives physical loss of powered-off, locked media; it does not extend to a running system where the volume is already unlocked.

options.text: It protects the data equally in both states, since LUKS encrypts continuously regardless of whether the volume is unlocked, when an unlocked volume leaves its files readable to any permitted process exactly as an unencrypted one would.
options.why: Once unlocked, the volume's files are readable as normal to permitted processes; encryption at rest specifically addresses the powered-off, locked case, not a running unlocked one.

options.text: It protects the network traffic the laptop last sent, in addition to the stored files.
options.why: Full disk encryption is a storage control; it has no bearing on data that already crossed the network, which is encryption in transit's domain.

options.text: It protects only the LUKS header, not the data volume itself.
options.why: The header wraps the volume key that protects the actual data; both matter, but the encryption's purpose is protecting the data volume, not merely the header in isolation.

items.rationale: Full disk encryption survives the physical loss of powered-off, locked hardware — a stolen laptop yields nothing without the passphrase.
